summary.text: For each prime p, the proof computes the numerator and denominator valuations as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor^2\) and \(\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r=1}^{\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor} r\lfloor\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor/r\rfloor\), respectively; the termwise bound of the latter inner sum by \(M^2\) also proves the denominator divides the numerator, so the quotient valuation is their difference. For \(m=np+j\) with \(0\le j<p\), every \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) for \(i\ge1\) equals \(\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\), making both valuation sums—and hence their difference—constant throughout the block.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\prod_{r=1}^{m}\gcd(j,r)
\quad\text{and}\quad
D(m)=\prod_{s=1}^{m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac ms\right\rfloor!\right)^s.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and derive formulas for its prime-adic valuation. We then show that those formulas do not change when an integer of the form \(np\) is replaced by \(np+k\), where \(0\le k<p\).

For a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of \(x\).

## 1. The valuation of the numerator

We claim that for every prime \(q\),
\[
v_q(N(m))=\sum_{i\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\tag{1}
\]
This is a finite sum, since its terms vanish once \(q^i>m\).

Indeed, valuations turn products into sums, and for positive integers \(j,r\),
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,r))=\min\bigl(v_q(j),v_q(r)\bigr).
\]
Consequently,
\[
v_q(N(m))
 =\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}
   \min\bigl(v_q(j),v_q(r)\bigr).
\]
For any nonnegative integers \(u,v\),
\[
\min(u,v)=\sum_{i\ge1}{\bf 1}_{i\le u}{\bf 1}_{i\le v}.
\]
Also, \(i\le v_q(j)\) is equivalent to \(q^i\mid j\). Therefore
\[
\min\bigl(v_q(j),v_q(r)\bigr)
 =\sum_{i\ge1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}.
\]
Interchanging these finite sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(N(m))
&=\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j}\right)
  \left(\sum_{r=1}^{m}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid r}\right)\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
because there are exactly \(\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(q^i\) between \(1\) and \(m\). This proves (1).

## 2. The valuation of the denominator

We next claim that
\[
v_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{s=1}^{\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor}
 s\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor}{s}\right\rfloor.
\tag{2}
\]
Again, only finitely many terms are nonzero.

First recall Legendre's formula
\[
v_q(t!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{3}
\]
For completeness, this follows by writing
\[
v_q(t!)=\sum_{u=1}^{t}v_q(u).
\]
Each multiple of \(q\) contributes at least one, each multiple of \(q^2\) contributes one additional unit, and so on. The number of multiples of \(q^i\) not exceeding \(t\) is \(\lfloor t/q^i\rfloor\), giving (3).

Using (3) and the fact that \(v_q(x^s)=s v_q(x)\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(m))
&=\sum_{s=1}^{m}s\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac ms\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{s=1}^{m}s\sum_{i\ge1}
  \left\lfloor
    \frac{\lfloor m/s\rfloor}{q^i}
  \right\rfloor\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{s=1}^{m}s
  \left\lfloor
    \frac{\lfloor m/s\rfloor}{q^i}
  \right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For positive integers \(u,v\), repeated integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/u\rfloor}{v}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m}{uv}\right\rfloor.
\]
It follows, using commutativity of multiplication, that
\[
\left\lfloor
  \frac{\lfloor m/s\rfloor}{q^i}
\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{s q^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor
  \frac{\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor}{s}
\right\rfloor.
\]
Put
\[
M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(s>M_i\), then \(\lfloor M_i/s\rfloor=0\), so the inner sum can be truncated at \(M_i\). Hence
\[
v_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{s=1}^{M_i}s\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{s}\right\rfloor,
\]
which is (2).

## 3. The quotient is an integer

For every nonnegative integer \(M\), define
\[
S(M)=\sum_{s=1}^{M}s\left\lfloor\frac Ms\right\rfloor.
\]
Each summand satisfies
\[
s\left\lfloor\frac Ms\right\rfloor\le M,
\]
because \(s\lfloor M/s\rfloor\) is the largest multiple of \(s\) not exceeding \(M\). Since there are \(M\) summands,
\[
S(M)\le M^2.
\tag{4}
\]

Apply this with \(M=M_i=\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\). Equations (1), (2), and (4) give, for every prime \(q\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(m))
&=\sum_{i\ge1}S(M_i)\\
&\le\sum_{i\ge1}M_i^2\\
&=v_q(N(m)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Both \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\) are positive integers. By unique prime factorization, a positive integer divides another precisely when its valuation at every prime is no greater. Thus
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\tag{5}
\]
In particular, \(a(m)=N(m)/D(m)\) is an integer. Moreover, from (5),
\[
v_q(a(m))=v_q(N(m))-v_q(D(m)).
\tag{6}
\]
Combining (1), (2), and (6), one could write an explicit formula for \(v_q(a(m))\); for the conjecture, it is enough to observe that both the numerator and denominator valuations depend only on the collection of integers
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor,
\qquad i\ge1.
\tag{7}
\]

## 4. Constancy of the relevant floors on a block of length \(p\)

Now fix a positive integer \(n\), a prime \(p\), and an integer \(k\) satisfying
\[
0\le k<p.
\]
We prove that for every \(i\ge1\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{8}
\]

Divide \(np\) by \(p^i\), writing
\[
np=p^i Q+r,
\qquad 0\le r<p^i.
\]
Because \(p\mid np\) and \(p\mid p^i\), we also have \(p\mid r\). Thus \(r\) is a multiple of \(p\). The largest multiple of \(p\) strictly below \(p^i\) is \(p^i-p\), so
\[
r\le p^i-p.
\]
Since \(k<p\), we have \(k\le p-1\), and therefore
\[
r+k\le(p^i-p)+(p-1)=p^i-1<p^i.
\]
It follows that
\[
np+k=p^iQ+(r+k)

defines the same quotient \(Q\) upon division by \(p^i\) as does \(np\). This proves (8).

## 5. Equality of valuations

Take \(q=p\) in the numerator formula (1). By (8), every corresponding summand is equal for \(m=np\) and \(m=np+k\):
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\]
Hence
\[
v_p(N(np+k))=v_p(N(np)).
\tag{9}
\]

Likewise, formula (2) expresses \(v_p(D(m))\) entirely in terms of the values
\(M_i=\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\). By (8), these values are unchanged when \(m=np\) is replaced by \(np+k\). Therefore
\[
v_p(D(np+k))=v_p(D(np)).
\tag{10}
\]

Finally, apply the quotient valuation formula (6) at \(m=np\) and at \(m=np+k\). Using (9) and (10),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(np+k))
&=v_p(N(np+k))-v_p(D(np+k))\\
&=v_p(N(np))-v_p(D(np))\\
&=v_p(a(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
=\cdots=
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as required.
